title: Help my unbelief (Mark 9:14–29)
hook: a desperate father: I believe; help my unbelief

segments.voice: Yesterday, on the mountain, a voice from the cloud gave one instruction. Your line was listen to him. Did you manage to listen more than you spoke? Day one hundred ninety-six. The end of another week.

From the shining mountain straight down into a mess. At the bottom there's a crowd, and an argument. The disciples who stayed behind have tried to heal a boy, and they couldn't. The boy's father pushes through. His son, he says, has a spirit that takes his speech, throws him to the ground, makes him foam and grind his teeth and go rigid. Since he was a child. It has thrown him into fire and into water. Years of nights like that, and now even the disciples have failed. So when he gets to Jesus, his hope is worn thin. In the King James Bible he says: "if thou canst do any thing, have compassion on us, and help us." If.
screen: `DOWN FROM THE MOUNTAIN.` → `THE DISCIPLES COULDN'T.` → `IF THOU CANST DO ANY THING.`

segments.voice: Jesus catches the word and hands the if back. In the King James text: "If thou canst believe, all things are possible to him that believeth." And the father cries out, with tears: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Both at once. I believe, and I don't. I trust you, and I'm terrified. He doesn't pretend. And Jesus doesn't send him away to come back when his faith is tidier. He heals the boy, and lifts him by the hand. In Mark's telling, half a faith, handed over honestly, is where it starts. The Greek word for unbelief is apistia, faith with a no in front of it. Some Christians call this verse a lifeline, because it puts doubt and faith in the same heart, in the same sentence. Readers today often notice that the boy's signs sound like epilepsy. Mark describes a spirit, and Christians understand stories like this in different ways; the text simply tells it as a spirit. Later, the disciples ask privately why they failed. His answer, in the King James: "This kind can come forth by nothing, but by prayer and fasting." Now look back at the week. Seven baskets: enough again. Hard hearts in a boat: do you not yet understand? A blind man seeing men like trees. Peter: you are the Christ. Take up your cross. Listen to him. And now this father. Again and again this week, someone sees in part, and is helped further along.
screen: `IF THOU CANST?` · `I BELIEVE; HELP MY UNBELIEF.` · `BY PRAYER AND FASTING.` · `A WEEK OF SEEING IN PART.` · then, large: `LORD, I BELIEVE; HELP THOU MINE UNBELIEF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold both halves honestly. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you trust, and one thing you doubt. About God, about yourself, about someone you love. Don't solve either one. Just let them sit side by side. If you pray, you can say the father's words, slowly, as many times as you like: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. If you don't pray, you can simply say: some of me trusts, some of me doesn't, and that's where I am. The bell holds the time.
Help my unbelief. A father's prayer with belief and doubt in one breath, and it was enough.
Your line: help my unbelief. Today, when you feel only half sure, don't wait to be certain. Bring the half you have. Day one hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Some Christians pray the father's words, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief," as a short prayer in times of doubt, and some pastors point to this story to say that faith and doubt can live together.

original.note: Greek: unbelief. pistis, faith, with a- in front: not.

trapdoor: what you thought: faith means never doubting.
what it means: a father holds belief and doubt together, says so, and Jesus answers him anyway.
what a scholar hears: apistia, un-faith: pistis, faith, with a no in front. belief and its opposite in one cry.

notes: Mark 9:29: 'and fasting' is absent from Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; stated as 'the oldest Greek manuscripts'. Confirm.

The note that the boy's signs resemble epilepsy is a common modern observation (Matthew 17:15 uses a word often rendered 'lunatick'/epileptic). Handled without ranking readings; Keeper to confirm tone.
